articles.title: How to Shape Insurance Claims Retrieval Architecture: 5 Access Rules for Auditable Intake
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every handoff. For an insurance claims intake system, that usually means separa…
articles.body: Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every handoff. For an insurance claims intake system, that usually means separating policy wording, claim evidence, and operational rules, then recording which collection and document version produced each answer. The bill is mostly a retention decision, not a search-engine decision. Keeping every OCR fragment, duplicate attachment, and superseded endorsement in the hot retrieval set increases index work and makes reviewers inspect noise. A deliberate re-index policy, plus removal of deleted records, changes that dominant term.

articles.excerpt: Automating PR-Based Development with Claude Task Master Claude Task Master (claudetm) is a command line tool that keeps Claude working until a goal is achieved. It is built on the Claude Agent SDK and…
articles.body: Automating PR-Based Development with Claude Task Master Claude Task Master ( claudetm ) is a command line tool that keeps Claude working until a goal is achieved. It is built on the Claude Agent SDK and follows a strict PR-based workflow. This article explains how to set up the tool, how it orchestrates tasks, and how you can extend it with its REST API and webhook system. Core Concepts The tool operates in a loop that consists of four stages: planning, working, PR lifecycle, and verification. In the planning stage it reads the codebase, creates a task list and defines success criteria. During the working stage it makes code changes, runs tests, commits and pushes each change. The PR lifecycle stage opens a pull request, waits for CI, fixes failures and addresses review comments.

articles.title: Mirroring an Android Phone to a Mac
articles.excerpt: Sometimes you want to see and control your Android phone's screen right on your Mac, wirelessly. Here's the whole setup in a few steps. adb and scrcpy installed (brew install android-platform-tools sc…
articles.body: Sometimes you want to see and control your Android phone's screen right on your Mac, wirelessly. Here's the whole setup in a few steps. What you need adb and scrcpy installed ( brew install android-platform-tools scrcpy on Mac) Developer Options + USB debugging enabled on the phone Phone and Mac on the same Wi-Fi network Connect over Wi-Fi Plug the phone in via USB once, then switch adb to wireless mode: adb tcpip 5555 Find the phone's IP (Settings → About phone → Status, or adb shell ip addr ), then connect: adb connect <phone-ip>:5555 Confirm it's attached: adb devices -l Note: If adb connect times out, it's usually a stale/wrong IP — phones often switch Wi-Fi networks or get a new DHCP lease. Re-check the IP on the phone and retry.

articles.title: Why we built ServerOS around the servers you already own
articles.excerpt: Today the ServerOS team is launching ServerOS in beta: one panel for the servers you already own. For years we've watched the same thing happen. A team starts with one server. Then there are five, acr…
articles.body: Today the ServerOS team is launching ServerOS in beta: one panel for the servers you already own. The problem For years we've watched the same thing happen. A team starts with one server. Then there are five, across three providers. Someone set up the backups, maybe. Nobody is quite sure what's running on the old box, or what happens if it goes down at 2am. The usual answer is to move everything onto a new platform. Most teams don't want that. They already have servers that work. They just want to see them, look after them and stop worrying about them. What ServerOS does One-command install on any Linux server, from any provider. Discovery: it finds what's already running (containers, services, databases, scheduled jobs).

articles.excerpt: A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (in blue) and…
articles.body: NASA A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (in blue) and Victor “Ike” Glover (in green) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) Jeremy Hansen (in red) observed impact flashes and their locations, which are noted on the image. Overall, the astronauts reported seeing five extremely faint “pinprick” bursts of light from their view aboard Orion, which was 46,000 miles away from the Moon at the time. These flashes are sparked by rocky fragments hitting the Moon.
